subject: Mathematics
board: Pearson Edexcel Level 1/Level 2 GCSE (9-1) in Mathematics (1MA1)

lessons.title: Randomness, fairness and expected frequency
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we tell whether a game is fair, and how many wins should we expect?
objectives: Decide whether outcomes are equally likely and whether a process is fair
Use expected frequency = number of trials x probability
Judge whether results suggest a biased die or spinner
successCriteria: All: say whether a die or spinner is fair and find a probability from equally likely outcomes
Some: explain whether results are evidence of bias
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: fair tests and random sampling
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and honesty (adl) in games and in dealing with others

keywords.def: each outcome is uncertain and cannot be predicted in advance
outcomes that each have the same chance of happening
describes a process where all outcomes are equally likely
not fair: some outcomes are more likely than others
how many times we expect an outcome in a number of trials: n x p

starter: Bismillah. Write 3/10 as a decimal and as a percentage.
A bag has 3 red and 7 blue counters. What is P(red)?
Why must probabilities of all outcomes add to 1?

teach.heading: Random and equally likely
bullets: Random: each outcome is uncertain, so we cannot predict one result.
Equally likely: every outcome has the same chance.
Equally likely outcomes give P(event) = favourable / total.
teach.note: Ask pupils for examples of random things (a coin toss) and not-random things (the sun rising). Stress that random does not mean equally likely: a weather forecast of rain is random but not 50:50. Use a fair six-sided die: six equally likely outcomes so P(5) = 1/6, P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

teach.heading: Is it fair?
bullets: A fair process gives every outcome the same chance.
Spinner with sections 180, 90, 45, 45 degrees: not fair.
teach.note: Draw both spinners. For the unfair one, probabilities are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 - they still add to 1. A game is fair if each player has the same chance of winning. Example: player A wins on 1-3, player B wins on 4-6 on a fair die. Fair. Ask: is it fair if A wins on 1 or 2 and B wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6?

teach.heading: Expected frequency
bullets: Expected frequency = number of trials x probability.
It is an average, not a promise.
Actual results usually differ from the expected value.
teach.note: Introduce with a fair die rolled 120 times: expected 6s = 120 x 1/6 = 20. Be clear that exactly 20 sixes would be surprising. The word expected means the average over many repeats. Link to the previous lesson on the sum of probabilities.

model.problem: A spinner lands on blue with probability 0.3. It is spun 200 times. How many times would you expect blue?
steps: Expected frequency = number of spins x probability

teach.heading: Evidence of bias?
teach.note: Table: a die rolled 60 times gave 1:6, 2:8, 3:9, 4:10, 5:11, 6:16. A fair die would give 10 of each. Six is 6 more than expected, but with only 60 rolls this could be chance. Teach the habit: compare with expected, say whether the difference is big, and say that more trials give stronger evidence. Do not say a die is definitely biased from 60 rolls.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer is B. A: wrong, 1/2 would be if there were two equally likely outcomes. C: probabilities need not be nice fractions. Use mini-whiteboards.

check.q: A fair 8-sided die is rolled 400 times. How many times would you expect a score of 8?
check.why: P(8) = 1/8, so expected = 400 x 1/8 = 50. 200 comes from using 1/2, and 5 divides the wrong way round.

practice: A fair spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. Write P(odd). Spun 150 times, how many odds are expected?
A game: roll a fair die. Aisha wins on 1 or 2, Bilal on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is it fair? Explain.
independent: Core: A fair die is rolled 90 times. Work out the expected number of (a) 4s (b) numbers greater than 4. A coin is flipped 50 times: expected heads?
Extend: P(red) = 0.35 on a spinner. In 240 spins, how many reds are expected? Why might the actual number be different? (2 marks)
Stretch: A 4-sided spinner landed on 1,2,3,4: 12, 18, 20, 30 times in 80 spins. Is there evidence the spinner is biased? Give a reasoned answer. (3 marks)
exit: A bag has 4 red and 6 green counters. One is picked at random. Is picking red or green equally likely? Explain.
A coin lands on heads 18 times in 30 flips. Is it definitely biased? Explain.
lessons.homework: Design a fair game for two players using two coins. Show that each player has the same chance of winning.
lessons.send: SEND: use real dice and a pre-drawn expected-frequency table. EAL: key words matched to pictures. Stretch: explain why a result far from expected may still be possible for a fair die.

lessons.title: Bigger samples, better estimates: relative frequency and theoretical probability
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do casinos and insurers rely on large numbers of trials?
objectives: Calculate relative frequency from experimental results
Explain that larger unbiased samples tend towards the theoretical probability
Estimate probabilities from experiments and use them for predictions
successCriteria: Most: choose the best estimate from several experiments
Some: combine sample results and explain the effect of sample size
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: repeating experiments to improve reliability
lessons.smsc: Social: using fair evidence rather than guesswork (truthfulness)

keywords.def: number of times an outcome occurs divided by number of trials
the probability worked out from equally likely outcomes
a sample chosen with no outcome favoured
a best guess based on evidence

starter: Bismillah. A fair die is rolled 300 times. How many 3s expected?
Write 0.35 as a fraction in simplest form.

teach.heading: Relative frequency
bullets: Relative frequency = frequency of outcome / total trials.
It is an estimate of probability from an experiment.
Give as a fraction or decimal.
teach.note: Recall that theoretical probability needs equally likely outcomes. When outcomes are not equally likely (a bent coin, a drawing pin landing point up) we find probability by experiment. A pin lands point up 14 times in 40: relative frequency 14/40 = 0.35.

teach.heading: What happens as trials increase?
teach.note: Show the table. A fair coin has P(heads) = 0.5. Relative frequencies: 10 trials 7 heads gives 0.7; 50 trials 28 heads gives 0.56; 200 trials 104 gives 0.52; 1000 trials 507 gives 0.507. They settle near 0.5. Say: the early values wobble, the later ones are close. This tendency, not a guarantee, is the key idea.

teach.heading: Large samples: but only if unbiased
bullets: More trials usually gives a better estimate.
The experiment must be fair: no cheating or bias.
Small samples can be far from the true value.
teach.note: Discuss why the sample must be unbiased: if a coin is flipped by someone who flips it carefully to land heads, 10000 trials will not give 0.5. Also contrast: relative frequency gets closer to the true probability, but the number of heads does not become exactly half. After 1000 flips, 507 is 7 away from 500; the difference in the count can grow while the proportion settles.

teach.heading: Combining and using results
teach.note: Walk through. Total trials 40 + 160 = 200. Total successes 12 + 52 = 64. Relative frequency 64/200 = 0.32. Use the larger sample (more trials) if you must choose one, but combining is best. Then use it: in 500 more trials, expect 500 x 0.32 = 160.

model.problem: A biased spinner: in 40 spins it landed on red 12 times. In a further 160 spins it landed on red 52 times. Estimate P(red) and the expected number of reds in 500 spins.
model.answer: P(red) is about 0.32; expect about 160 reds

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Pupils often choose the largest number of reds or say the average of the two decimals. A is tempting because 0.5 is theoretical.

check.q: Three people test a coin. Amy: 20 flips, 14 heads. Ben: 200 flips, 108 heads. Cara: 50 flips, 26 heads. Whose results give the best estimate of P(heads)?
check.why: A larger unbiased sample tends to be closer to the true probability. Ben used 200 flips; relative frequency 0.54.

practice: A drawing pin was dropped 80 times and landed point up 52 times. Find the relative frequency. Expected number point up in 300 drops?
Table of relative frequencies for a die showing 6: 10 rolls 0.3; 100 rolls 0.19; 1000 rolls 0.168. What do they suggest about P(6)?
independent: Core: A coin was flipped 40 times with 22 heads. Write the relative frequency of heads as a decimal.
Extend: Sam rolled a die 60 times and got 15 sixes; Tia rolled it 600 times and got 108 sixes. Whose estimate of P(six) is better? Explain. (3 marks)
Stretch: A spinner has red, blue, green. In 400 spins: red 148, blue 160, green 92. Estimate P(green), then estimate the number of blues in 1500 spins. (4 marks)
exit: Why is relative frequency from 1000 trials usually more reliable than from 10?
A fair die gave 4 sixes in 10 rolls. Does that mean the die is biased?
lessons.homework: Flip a coin 20 times, record the relative frequency after 5, 10 and 20 flips, and write one sentence about what you notice.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-filled running-total tables and a calculator. EAL: sentence stem 'As the number of trials increases...'. Stretch: explain why the count of heads need not equal half the trials.
